medical.title: Malaria remains the leading cause of hospital admission and in-hospital death in children under 2 in Sierra Leone
medical.summary: Malaria, respiratory infections and diarrhea are the leading causes of hospitalization and death during the first two years of life in Sierra Leone, according to a prospective study led by ISGlobal, a center supported by the "la Caixa" Foundation. The findings, obtained as part of the ICARIA project and published in The Lancet Global Health, show that, despite the implementation of the main preventive strategies currently available, Sierra Leone continues to have one of the highest child mortality rates in the world.

medical.title: Researchers identify high-IgA MASLD subtype linked to liver-related events
medical.summary: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a common liver condition that can follow very different paths among patients. Although fibrosis is a key indicator, some patients without advanced fibrosis can still develop serious liver-related events. This variation led researchers to investigate whether distinct clinical subtypes of MASLD could reveal additional clues about disease progression and risk.

medical.title: How the benefits of vaccination extend beyond protection from infection
medical.summary: Vaccination not only prevents disease caused by acute infection but also protects against long-term immune-related sequelae that can follow an acute viral infection. This is the main conclusion of a study led by the Infection Biology Laboratory at Pompeu Fabra University.

medical.title: Nasal vaccine additive improves flu survival in mice even 100 days after treatment
medical.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic showed the challenges of protecting populations when a new respiratory virus emerges. Although vaccines were developed at unprecedented speed, there was still a period when vaccines were not yet available, and people remained vulnerable to infection. This raises an important question: Could the body's natural defenses be temporarily strengthened without knowing which virus will emerge?

medical.title: New research reveals the remarkable complexity of human milk
medical.summary: Two major international studies are providing new insight into how human milk is regulated, showing that some components respond to maternal nutrition, while others remain stable or reflect biological processes involved in lactation and infant growth.

medical.title: Blood cells from 80-year-old donor become stem cells with molecular age under 20
medical.summary: Researchers from the University Hospital of Bonn and the University of Bonn have succeeded in dramatically rejuvenating human cells in a test tube. To do so, they directly reprogrammed red blood cell precursors into stem cells from which neurons can be derived. During this process, the molecular clocks that indicate a cell's age were reset. For example, blood cells from an 80-year-old were transformed into stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20 years.

medical.title: The gut‑muscle link: Why fermented foods could boost muscle health
medical.summary: Gut health and muscle health are often thought of as separate concerns. The first brings to mind eating fiber and probiotics, while the other centers on exercise and protein.

medical.title: Lab-grown blood vessels reveal roles of different cells in rapid-aging disease
medical.summary: Biomedical engineers at Duke University have developed a three-layer model of human blood vessels that enables researchers to better understand how Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS), a rare genetic disorder that causes accelerated aging, affects the vascular system.

medical.title: Deep learning model using ECGs during sleep studies can predict cardiovascular outcomes
medical.summary: A research team supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has found that electrocardiograms (ECGs) administered during sleep and paired with sleep stage information can be used to determine the risk of future adverse cardiac events. The study, which used a deep learning approach, suggests that using ECGs to predict which patients have a greater risk of poor heart-related outcomes could help guide clinical decision-making. The findings were published in the journal SLEEP.

medical.title: Certain diets are linked to better cognitive performance, new study finds
medical.summary: The 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee weighed the available evidence on dietary patterns associated with the risk of cognitive impairment and dementia but said there were not enough data to make a recommendation. In response, a new paper by U.S. and European researchers addresses ambiguities across studies and harmonizes key data to shed light on how different diets may shape cognitive performance, executive function and dementia.

medical.title: Students from military families are often misunderstood in US public schools—experts explain what schools can do
medical.summary: Over 1.4 million children had a parent or caregiver who served in the U.S. armed forces in 2024.

medical.title: Alternative signaling pathway improves transplantation of blood stem cells
medical.summary: Blood stem cells are rare cells in the bone marrow that produce the blood and immune cells needed throughout life, ensuring that the body's blood and immune system are renewed. This is why they are also used in bone marrow transplants and novel gene therapies for treating a range of blood disorders. However, during gene therapy, the stem cells need to be processed in the laboratory before transplantation, which can cause them to lose some of their regenerative capacity and reduce the chance of the overall treatment being successful.

medical.title: Olive oil-based lotion could simplify scabies treatment by clearing mites and eggs with a single application
medical.summary: Every year, around 400 million people worldwide are affected by an intensely itchy skin condition caused by microscopic parasitic mites called Sarcoptes scabiei. Known as scabies, the infestation begins when the tiny mites burrow into the top layer of the skin, where they live and lay eggs. This triggers severe itching, inflammation, rash-like lesions and crusting. In a recent study, researchers developed a single topical treatment that targets both live mites and their eggs, something most conventional medications fail to do.

medical.title: Why do runners get so many injuries? And does strength training really make a difference?
medical.summary: For many of us, running is one of the most accessible forms of exercise. It's free, and you don't need equipment. But it is also one of the forms of exercise more likely to lead to injury.

medical.title: First real-world study of safety and quality of patient-facing AI in primary care
medical.summary: The aging population, workforce changes and patients' increasingly complex medical needs are all factors straining primary care systems around the world. Artificial intelligence tools have emerged as a potential means of extending the capabilities of health care workers, including in primary care settings. Large language models (LLMs), also known as chatbots, have performed extremely well in simulations. However, little is known about how these systems perform with real patients.

medical.title: New tool helps women decide if egg freezing is right for them
medical.summary: Egg freezing is on the rise. More than 22,000 women in Australia and New Zealand underwent elective egg freezing between 2009 and 2023. Uptake has increased sharply, and there's little sign it will slow down anytime soon.

medical.title: Your gut bacteria may reveal how fast your brain is aging
medical.summary: A UCLA study links faster brain aging to specific gut bacteria and chemical byproducts, with older-looking brains also associated with poorer memory, focus, and mood. The findings suggest that biological signs of brain aging may appear decades before obvious symptoms and could eventually make the gut a target for prevention.

medical.title: Diet drinks work as well as water for weight loss, major trial finds
medical.summary: A two-year randomized clinical trial involving 493 adults with overweight or obesity found that diet soft drinks were essentially as effective as water for long-term weight loss and weight maintenance. Participants drinking beverages sweetened with aspartame, acesulfame-K, or sucralose lost a similar amount of weight to those drinking water, while both groups also saw improvements in waist size, body composition, and several metabolic measures.

medical.title: Hidden stem cells may be fueling spinal stenosis
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a stem cell that appears to serve as a master source for tendon and ligament cells throughout the body. In lumbar spinal stenosis, these cells become unusually active and may drive the ligament overgrowth that squeezes spinal nerves and causes pain, numbness, and difficulty walking. Researchers found that reducing calcium signaling stopped this abnormal growth in mice.

medical.title: Scientists find new virus behind mysterious tick illness
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a new tick-borne virus in China that causes flu-like illness and may account for previously unexplained cases of fever, fatigue, digestive problems, and low platelet counts. Most patients with ALTNV alone recovered, but coinfections with another dangerous tick-borne virus were linked to more serious complications.

science.title: Cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation—it functions as an extension of school violence, say researchers
science.summary: A new study of 4,200 adolescents revealed that cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation; it almost always functions as an extension of physical and verbal aggression already present in the school environment. The study, conducted at the Federal University of São Paulo (Unifesp) in Brazil, mapped students' involvement in bullying and found that the lines between victims and perpetrators often blur in a cycle of violence spanning both the physical and digital worlds.

science.title: What a swordfish washing up on British Columbia's coast says about our changing oceans
science.summary: Filmmaker and outdoorsperson Quinn Barabash recently made headlines when he found a swordfish carcass nearly two meters (6.6 feet) long on the remote shores of Haida Gwaii in northern British Columbia.

science.title: Nightjar wings reveal a trade-off between hunting slowly and traveling far
science.summary: The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nocturnal migratory bird that travels between Europe and southern Africa each year. However, its wings are not only used for long-distance journeys. When hunting insects, the nightjar must be able to slow down, turn sharply and fly at low speeds. Researchers at Lund University have now shown how this trade-off is reflected in the bird's flight mechanics. The study is published in the journal PLOS Biology.

science.title: Genetic analysis reveals that some specialty coffee seeds do not match their commercial identity
science.summary: Genetic analysis revealed that several seeds from a batch sold as Sidra were not, in fact, Sidra; their genetic profile was closer to that of Batian, a Kenyan variety.

science.title: Q&A: How does AI affect our engagement at work?
science.summary: AI is being integrated into our work at a growing rate. Andreas Bergqvist, a Ph.D. student at the Department of Information Technology, has teamed up with colleagues to investigate how AI, automation and robotization affect work engagement.

science.title: 'Mix-and-match' material's properties can be tuned by changing its metallic 'recipe'
science.summary: Scientists have created a new family of materials whose behavior can be tuned by changing their metallic "recipe"—opening new possibilities for uses including gas storage and sensing.

science.title: Are analytics making pro sports less fun? Fans and analysts remain divided
science.summary: Today, the discussions of sports analytics in the 2011 movie "Moneyball" often seem quaint. The idea of a team using data to find players who may be more valuable than meets the eye (and less expensive) no longer surprises anyone.

science.title: New sensing method expands label-free particle detection beyond sensor surfaces
science.summary: Finding a single cancer cell in a tube of blood is a bit like finding a needle in a haystack. As researchers seek to detect ever-smaller and rarer targets, from viruses to circulating tumor cells in blood, the demand for ultrasensitive, robust sensors that are practical for real-world samples continues to grow.

science.title: AI reveals how coating thickness changes the link between surface roughness and pitting resistance
science.summary: Localized pitting corrosion can cause sudden failure in aluminum components even when overall corrosion rates are low. Steam coating offers a water-vapor-based route to protective boehmite films, but processing simultaneously changes film thickness, surface morphology, crystallinity and substrate defects.

science.title: Confidence in a relationship's future is linked to feelings of romantic security
science.summary: Feeling secure in a relationship is not only about how people connect with their partners today. It may also depend on how confident they are that the relationship will continue into the future. Feelings of closeness, trust and connection, together with a sense that the relationship is stable and has a future, can shape how people experience their romantic relationships.

science.title: Kīlauea's swelling summit helps scientists forecast lava fountain eruptions
science.summary: Episodic lava fountaining is a rare volcanic behavior in which repeated, hours-long bursts of molten lava and gas are spewed from volcanic vents, with quiet pauses lasting days to weeks between episodes. These lava fountains have been observed in active volcanoes in places like Hawaii, Iceland and Italy, but researchers still do not fully understand what starts, sustains or stops these individual fountain episodes.

science.title: African antelopes spreading in New Mexico: How far could they go under climate change?
science.summary: Majestic African antelopes known as gemsbok have been roaming the U.S. Southwest since their introduction in the 1960s and 1970s. Brought to New Mexico as a game species for hunting, gemsbok quickly settled in, expanding more than 100 kilometers (62 miles) from their introduction point. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers say that's due to their exceptional adaptations to arid conditions, which they predict will dramatically expand under climate change.

science.title: Why faculty diversity at universities still lags far behind the changing demographics of college students
science.summary: U.S. colleges and universities have long struggled to increase the racial diversity of their faculty.

science.title: Data centers make heat all year long—here's how the ground can hold onto it until winter
science.summary: You have probably noticed it on a hot summer day: A basement feels cool even when the air outside is baking. The ground does not heat up and cool down as fast as the air does. A few hundred feet down, it stays close to the local yearly average all year, which can be around 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius).

science.title: The oil market that sets today's gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
science.summary: The fall of 2026 is a moment when energy takes center stage, as geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans' everyday lives.

science.title: How plant enzymes learned to tell mirror-image molecules apart
science.summary: Many naturally occurring molecules such as menthol or limonene exist in two mirror-image forms, known as enantiomers, that look almost identical but can differ greatly in smell, taste or effect on the body.

science.title: Q&A: Investor perspective prompts auditors to rate CEO misconduct as more significant
science.summary: When thinking like investors, auditors are significantly more likely to rate corporate leaders' crimes as material concerns for the investing public, according to new Poole research. In their professional capacities, the study finds, auditors tend to rate executive lapses as less material to their firms' financial performance.

science.title: Tiny marine microbe sheds new light on how little genetic machinery a cell needs to survive
science.summary: Scientists have discovered a previously unknown microorganism that has the smallest genome ever found and may be able to replicate and express its own genetic information.

science.title: Light-responsive inks could make tattoos visible on demand, but safety remains unproven
science.summary: A team of engineers has designed a new line of multicolored tattoo inks that switch on and off with different kinds of light. Described in a study published in Matter & Light, the technology could one day help people hide their tattoos when they have an important business meeting. They could even doodle on their own skin using a simple laser pointer.

science.title: Light reads electron spins inside porous crystals, opening path to quantum chemical sensors
science.summary: University of Glasgow researchers are part of an international collaboration that could lead to a new generation of quantum sensors. The team, which included researchers from the University of Tokyo, University of Glasgow, University of Sheffield and Kobe University, has for the first time used light to read out the magnetic spin of electrons trapped inside a porous crystalline material known as a metal-organic framework (MOF).

science.title: New auditing rules are curbing international money moves, study suggests
science.summary: A new study suggests that expanded financial audit reporting is having a significant impact on the behavior of multinational corporations. Specifically, the study finds that requiring more detailed analysis in financial audits appears to be curbing the corporate practice of shifting money internationally to pay less in taxes.

science.title: Broken bones in ancient homes shed new light on Viking violence
science.summary: Fragmented bones and skull pieces found in hearths, beneath floors and in other domestic settings in early Scandinavian settlement sites are providing fresh insights into Iron Age and Viking Age violence.

science.title: From bogong moths to Christmas beetles—how to slow down and spot more insects
science.summary: Millions of people worldwide watched as the Sydney Olympics came to a close in 2000. Meanwhile, thousands of bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) were airborne, making their annual migration to the Australian Alps.

science.title: Ultrafast core-level spectroscopy reveals elusive precursors of exciton condensation in quantum materials
science.summary: Many fascinating phases in quantum materials emerge when electrons, atoms and other microscopic components begin to act collectively. But these phases do not necessarily appear out of nowhere when a material crosses a transition temperature. Before long-range order develops, microscopic fluctuations can already be present.

science.title: A meteor hit Oklahoma 100 million years later than scientists thought
science.summary: A meteor crater buried beneath Oklahoma has turned out to be nearly 100 million years younger than scientists thought. Zircon crystals show the Ames impact occurred about 370 million years ago, meaning it was not part of the mysterious Ordovician bombardment once linked to a possible ring of debris around Earth. Instead, the impact coincided closely with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.

environment.title: Activists cite ecological, social connections in blocking US border wall construction (commentary)
environment.summary: A group of activists in the small border town of Lochiel, Arizona, U.S., is fighting to save 200-year-old cottonwood trees by stopping contractors from building a section of the U.S.’s new wall along its border with Mexico. One activist lived for over 70 days in the upper branches of an ancient cottonwood dubbed the “Grandmother […]

environment.title: Crackdown reveals ‘industrial-scale’ wildlife and timber trafficking across Latin America
environment.summary: Authorities across nine Latin American and Caribbean countries have arrested hundreds of people and recovered more than 1,000 animals as part of a two-month coordinated operation against environmental crimes. Operation Madre Tierra was the eighth edition of a recurring Interpol-led initiative, and was conducted in June and July in Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, […]

The precarious rope dangled from the eighth-floor window of a motel room overlooking a dark alley in the South Korean port city of Busan, swinging left and right with the wind. The men had […]

environment.title: Australia’s new eco police flexes muscles with major wildlife trafficking bust
environment.summary: Australian authorities have disrupted an alleged wildlife trafficking syndicate, uncovering a clandestine operation where smuggled native animals were hoarded alongside caches of cash and gold, reports contributor Johan Augustin for Mongabay. The operation reportedly seized 28 native and a few exotic species alongside approximately A$300,000 (nearly $210,000) in cash, gold, and silver bullion on July […]

environment.title: Invasive species have more severe environmental impacts in Global South, study finds
environment.summary: The environmental impacts caused by invasive alien species are more severe in poor countries of Global South than wealthy countries of Global North, a new study finds. The study shatters a long-standing assumption that wealthier Global North countries suffer the worst effects of invasive alien species (IAS) and highlights weak governance and insufficient management capacity […]

environment.title: Did two of the lemurs stolen in Bangladesh end up in India? Officials are investigating
environment.summary: The case of three ring-tailed lemurs, an endangered species, stolen from Gazipur Safari Park in Bangladesh last year resurfaced on social media in September this year, when news spread that two of the lemurs were trafficked to India and later sheltered at a private wildlife conservation facility, Vantara. The viral news prompted Vantara to release […]

environment.title: Logging threatens Bornean forest earmarked for Indigenous Peace Park
environment.summary: Part of a forest in Malaysian Borneo that Indigenous communities had envisioned co-managing and self-governing has been turned into an active commercial logging concession, according to a recent civil society report. The 283,500-hectare (700,500-acre) Upper Baram Forest Area, in the northeastern part of the state of Sarawak, was proposed as a community-led conservation area more […]

environment.title: Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
environment.summary: A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.

mix_items.title: Malaria remains the leading cause of hospital admission and in-hospital death in children under 2 in Sierra Leone
mix_items.summary: Malaria, respiratory infections and diarrhea are the leading causes of hospitalization and death during the first two years of life in Sierra Leone, according to a prospective study led by ISGlobal, a center supported by the "la Caixa" Foundation. The findings, obtained as part of the ICARIA project and published in The Lancet Global Health, show that, despite the implementation of the main preventive strategies currently available, Sierra Leone continues to have one of the highest child mortality rates in the world.

mix_items.title: Cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation—it functions as an extension of school violence, say researchers
mix_items.summary: A new study of 4,200 adolescents revealed that cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation; it almost always functions as an extension of physical and verbal aggression already present in the school environment. The study, conducted at the Federal University of São Paulo (Unifesp) in Brazil, mapped students' involvement in bullying and found that the lines between victims and perpetrators often blur in a cycle of violence spanning both the physical and digital worlds.

mix_items.title: What a swordfish washing up on British Columbia's coast says about our changing oceans
mix_items.summary: Filmmaker and outdoorsperson Quinn Barabash recently made headlines when he found a swordfish carcass nearly two meters (6.6 feet) long on the remote shores of Haida Gwaii in northern British Columbia.

mix_items.title: Nightjar wings reveal a trade-off between hunting slowly and traveling far
mix_items.summary: The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nocturnal migratory bird that travels between Europe and southern Africa each year. However, its wings are not only used for long-distance journeys. When hunting insects, the nightjar must be able to slow down, turn sharply and fly at low speeds. Researchers at Lund University have now shown how this trade-off is reflected in the bird's flight mechanics. The study is published in the journal PLOS Biology.

mix_items.title: Genetic analysis reveals that some specialty coffee seeds do not match their commercial identity
mix_items.summary: Genetic analysis revealed that several seeds from a batch sold as Sidra were not, in fact, Sidra; their genetic profile was closer to that of Batian, a Kenyan variety.

mix_items.title: Q&A: How does AI affect our engagement at work?
mix_items.summary: AI is being integrated into our work at a growing rate. Andreas Bergqvist, a Ph.D. student at the Department of Information Technology, has teamed up with colleagues to investigate how AI, automation and robotization affect work engagement.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify high-IgA MASLD subtype linked to liver-related events
mix_items.summary: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a common liver condition that can follow very different paths among patients. Although fibrosis is a key indicator, some patients without advanced fibrosis can still develop serious liver-related events. This variation led researchers to investigate whether distinct clinical subtypes of MASLD could reveal additional clues about disease progression and risk.

mix_items.title: How the benefits of vaccination extend beyond protection from infection
mix_items.summary: Vaccination not only prevents disease caused by acute infection but also protects against long-term immune-related sequelae that can follow an acute viral infection. This is the main conclusion of a study led by the Infection Biology Laboratory at Pompeu Fabra University.

mix_items.title: 'Mix-and-match' material's properties can be tuned by changing its metallic 'recipe'
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a new family of materials whose behavior can be tuned by changing their metallic "recipe"—opening new possibilities for uses including gas storage and sensing.

mix_items.title: Nasal vaccine additive improves flu survival in mice even 100 days after treatment
mix_items.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic showed the challenges of protecting populations when a new respiratory virus emerges. Although vaccines were developed at unprecedented speed, there was still a period when vaccines were not yet available, and people remained vulnerable to infection. This raises an important question: Could the body's natural defenses be temporarily strengthened without knowing which virus will emerge?

mix_items.title: Are analytics making pro sports less fun? Fans and analysts remain divided
mix_items.summary: Today, the discussions of sports analytics in the 2011 movie "Moneyball" often seem quaint. The idea of a team using data to find players who may be more valuable than meets the eye (and less expensive) no longer surprises anyone.

mix_items.title: New sensing method expands label-free particle detection beyond sensor surfaces
mix_items.summary: Finding a single cancer cell in a tube of blood is a bit like finding a needle in a haystack. As researchers seek to detect ever-smaller and rarer targets, from viruses to circulating tumor cells in blood, the demand for ultrasensitive, robust sensors that are practical for real-world samples continues to grow.

mix_items.title: AI reveals how coating thickness changes the link between surface roughness and pitting resistance
mix_items.summary: Localized pitting corrosion can cause sudden failure in aluminum components even when overall corrosion rates are low. Steam coating offers a water-vapor-based route to protective boehmite films, but processing simultaneously changes film thickness, surface morphology, crystallinity and substrate defects.

mix_items.title: New research reveals the remarkable complexity of human milk
mix_items.summary: Two major international studies are providing new insight into how human milk is regulated, showing that some components respond to maternal nutrition, while others remain stable or reflect biological processes involved in lactation and infant growth.

mix_items.title: Confidence in a relationship's future is linked to feelings of romantic security
mix_items.summary: Feeling secure in a relationship is not only about how people connect with their partners today. It may also depend on how confident they are that the relationship will continue into the future. Feelings of closeness, trust and connection, together with a sense that the relationship is stable and has a future, can shape how people experience their romantic relationships.

mix_items.title: Blood cells from 80-year-old donor become stem cells with molecular age under 20
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University Hospital of Bonn and the University of Bonn have succeeded in dramatically rejuvenating human cells in a test tube. To do so, they directly reprogrammed red blood cell precursors into stem cells from which neurons can be derived. During this process, the molecular clocks that indicate a cell's age were reset. For example, blood cells from an 80-year-old were transformed into stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20 years.

mix_items.title: Kīlauea's swelling summit helps scientists forecast lava fountain eruptions
mix_items.summary: Episodic lava fountaining is a rare volcanic behavior in which repeated, hours-long bursts of molten lava and gas are spewed from volcanic vents, with quiet pauses lasting days to weeks between episodes. These lava fountains have been observed in active volcanoes in places like Hawaii, Iceland and Italy, but researchers still do not fully understand what starts, sustains or stops these individual fountain episodes.

mix_items.title: The gut‑muscle link: Why fermented foods could boost muscle health
mix_items.summary: Gut health and muscle health are often thought of as separate concerns. The first brings to mind eating fiber and probiotics, while the other centers on exercise and protein.

mix_items.title: African antelopes spreading in New Mexico: How far could they go under climate change?
mix_items.summary: Majestic African antelopes known as gemsbok have been roaming the U.S. Southwest since their introduction in the 1960s and 1970s. Brought to New Mexico as a game species for hunting, gemsbok quickly settled in, expanding more than 100 kilometers (62 miles) from their introduction point. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers say that's due to their exceptional adaptations to arid conditions, which they predict will dramatically expand under climate change.

mix_items.title: Why faculty diversity at universities still lags far behind the changing demographics of college students
mix_items.summary: U.S. colleges and universities have long struggled to increase the racial diversity of their faculty.

mix_items.title: Lab-grown blood vessels reveal roles of different cells in rapid-aging disease
mix_items.summary: Biomedical engineers at Duke University have developed a three-layer model of human blood vessels that enables researchers to better understand how Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS), a rare genetic disorder that causes accelerated aging, affects the vascular system.

mix_items.title: Data centers make heat all year long—here's how the ground can hold onto it until winter
mix_items.summary: You have probably noticed it on a hot summer day: A basement feels cool even when the air outside is baking. The ground does not heat up and cool down as fast as the air does. A few hundred feet down, it stays close to the local yearly average all year, which can be around 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius).

mix_items.title: Deep learning model using ECGs during sleep studies can predict cardiovascular outcomes
mix_items.summary: A research team supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has found that electrocardiograms (ECGs) administered during sleep and paired with sleep stage information can be used to determine the risk of future adverse cardiac events. The study, which used a deep learning approach, suggests that using ECGs to predict which patients have a greater risk of poor heart-related outcomes could help guide clinical decision-making. The findings were published in the journal SLEEP.

mix_items.title: The oil market that sets today's gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
mix_items.summary: The fall of 2026 is a moment when energy takes center stage, as geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans' everyday lives.

mix_items.title: Certain diets are linked to better cognitive performance, new study finds
mix_items.summary: The 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee weighed the available evidence on dietary patterns associated with the risk of cognitive impairment and dementia but said there were not enough data to make a recommendation. In response, a new paper by U.S. and European researchers addresses ambiguities across studies and harmonizes key data to shed light on how different diets may shape cognitive performance, executive function and dementia.

mix_items.title: How plant enzymes learned to tell mirror-image molecules apart
mix_items.summary: Many naturally occurring molecules such as menthol or limonene exist in two mirror-image forms, known as enantiomers, that look almost identical but can differ greatly in smell, taste or effect on the body.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Investor perspective prompts auditors to rate CEO misconduct as more significant
mix_items.summary: When thinking like investors, auditors are significantly more likely to rate corporate leaders' crimes as material concerns for the investing public, according to new Poole research. In their professional capacities, the study finds, auditors tend to rate executive lapses as less material to their firms' financial performance.

mix_items.title: Students from military families are often misunderstood in US public schools—experts explain what schools can do
mix_items.summary: Over 1.4 million children had a parent or caregiver who served in the U.S. armed forces in 2024.

mix_items.title: Tiny marine microbe sheds new light on how little genetic machinery a cell needs to survive
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a previously unknown microorganism that has the smallest genome ever found and may be able to replicate and express its own genetic information.

mix_items.title: Light-responsive inks could make tattoos visible on demand, but safety remains unproven
mix_items.summary: A team of engineers has designed a new line of multicolored tattoo inks that switch on and off with different kinds of light. Described in a study published in Matter & Light, the technology could one day help people hide their tattoos when they have an important business meeting. They could even doodle on their own skin using a simple laser pointer.

mix_items.title: Alternative signaling pathway improves transplantation of blood stem cells
mix_items.summary: Blood stem cells are rare cells in the bone marrow that produce the blood and immune cells needed throughout life, ensuring that the body's blood and immune system are renewed. This is why they are also used in bone marrow transplants and novel gene therapies for treating a range of blood disorders. However, during gene therapy, the stem cells need to be processed in the laboratory before transplantation, which can cause them to lose some of their regenerative capacity and reduce the chance of the overall treatment being successful.

mix_items.title: Light reads electron spins inside porous crystals, opening path to quantum chemical sensors
mix_items.summary: University of Glasgow researchers are part of an international collaboration that could lead to a new generation of quantum sensors. The team, which included researchers from the University of Tokyo, University of Glasgow, University of Sheffield and Kobe University, has for the first time used light to read out the magnetic spin of electrons trapped inside a porous crystalline material known as a metal-organic framework (MOF).

mix_items.title: New auditing rules are curbing international money moves, study suggests
mix_items.summary: A new study suggests that expanded financial audit reporting is having a significant impact on the behavior of multinational corporations. Specifically, the study finds that requiring more detailed analysis in financial audits appears to be curbing the corporate practice of shifting money internationally to pay less in taxes.

mix_items.title: Olive oil-based lotion could simplify scabies treatment by clearing mites and eggs with a single application
mix_items.summary: Every year, around 400 million people worldwide are affected by an intensely itchy skin condition caused by microscopic parasitic mites called Sarcoptes scabiei. Known as scabies, the infestation begins when the tiny mites burrow into the top layer of the skin, where they live and lay eggs. This triggers severe itching, inflammation, rash-like lesions and crusting. In a recent study, researchers developed a single topical treatment that targets both live mites and their eggs, something most conventional medications fail to do.

mix_items.title: Broken bones in ancient homes shed new light on Viking violence
mix_items.summary: Fragmented bones and skull pieces found in hearths, beneath floors and in other domestic settings in early Scandinavian settlement sites are providing fresh insights into Iron Age and Viking Age violence.

mix_items.title: Why do runners get so many injuries? And does strength training really make a difference?
mix_items.summary: For many of us, running is one of the most accessible forms of exercise. It's free, and you don't need equipment. But it is also one of the forms of exercise more likely to lead to injury.

mix_items.title: First real-world study of safety and quality of patient-facing AI in primary care
mix_items.summary: The aging population, workforce changes and patients' increasingly complex medical needs are all factors straining primary care systems around the world. Artificial intelligence tools have emerged as a potential means of extending the capabilities of health care workers, including in primary care settings. Large language models (LLMs), also known as chatbots, have performed extremely well in simulations. However, little is known about how these systems perform with real patients.

mix_items.title: From bogong moths to Christmas beetles—how to slow down and spot more insects
mix_items.summary: Millions of people worldwide watched as the Sydney Olympics came to a close in 2000. Meanwhile, thousands of bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) were airborne, making their annual migration to the Australian Alps.

mix_items.title: Ultrafast core-level spectroscopy reveals elusive precursors of exciton condensation in quantum materials
mix_items.summary: Many fascinating phases in quantum materials emerge when electrons, atoms and other microscopic components begin to act collectively. But these phases do not necessarily appear out of nowhere when a material crosses a transition temperature. Before long-range order develops, microscopic fluctuations can already be present.

mix_items.title: New tool helps women decide if egg freezing is right for them
mix_items.summary: Egg freezing is on the rise. More than 22,000 women in Australia and New Zealand underwent elective egg freezing between 2009 and 2023. Uptake has increased sharply, and there's little sign it will slow down anytime soon.

mix_items.title: Activists cite ecological, social connections in blocking US border wall construction (commentary)
mix_items.summary: A group of activists in the small border town of Lochiel, Arizona, U.S., is fighting to save 200-year-old cottonwood trees by stopping contractors from building a section of the U.S.’s new wall along its border with Mexico. One activist lived for over 70 days in the upper branches of an ancient cottonwood dubbed the “Grandmother […]

mix_items.title: Crackdown reveals ‘industrial-scale’ wildlife and timber trafficking across Latin America
mix_items.summary: Authorities across nine Latin American and Caribbean countries have arrested hundreds of people and recovered more than 1,000 animals as part of a two-month coordinated operation against environmental crimes. Operation Madre Tierra was the eighth edition of a recurring Interpol-led initiative, and was conducted in June and July in Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, […]

mix_items.summary: SEOUL — At 2 a.m. one night, two Indonesian fishers were gripping a flimsy, makeshift rope, hanging on for dear life. The precarious rope dangled from the eighth-floor window of a motel room overlooking a dark alley in the South Korean port city of Busan, swinging left and right with the wind. The men had […]

mix_items.title: Australia’s new eco police flexes muscles with major wildlife trafficking bust
mix_items.summary: Australian authorities have disrupted an alleged wildlife trafficking syndicate, uncovering a clandestine operation where smuggled native animals were hoarded alongside caches of cash and gold, reports contributor Johan Augustin for Mongabay. The operation reportedly seized 28 native and a few exotic species alongside approximately A$300,000 (nearly $210,000) in cash, gold, and silver bullion on July […]

mix_items.title: Invasive species have more severe environmental impacts in Global South, study finds
mix_items.summary: The environmental impacts caused by invasive alien species are more severe in poor countries of Global South than wealthy countries of Global North, a new study finds. The study shatters a long-standing assumption that wealthier Global North countries suffer the worst effects of invasive alien species (IAS) and highlights weak governance and insufficient management capacity […]

mix_items.title: Did two of the lemurs stolen in Bangladesh end up in India? Officials are investigating
mix_items.summary: The case of three ring-tailed lemurs, an endangered species, stolen from Gazipur Safari Park in Bangladesh last year resurfaced on social media in September this year, when news spread that two of the lemurs were trafficked to India and later sheltered at a private wildlife conservation facility, Vantara. The viral news prompted Vantara to release […]

mix_items.title: Logging threatens Bornean forest earmarked for Indigenous Peace Park
mix_items.summary: Part of a forest in Malaysian Borneo that Indigenous communities had envisioned co-managing and self-governing has been turned into an active commercial logging concession, according to a recent civil society report. The 283,500-hectare (700,500-acre) Upper Baram Forest Area, in the northeastern part of the state of Sarawak, was proposed as a community-led conservation area more […]

mix_items.title: A meteor hit Oklahoma 100 million years later than scientists thought
mix_items.summary: A meteor crater buried beneath Oklahoma has turned out to be nearly 100 million years younger than scientists thought. Zircon crystals show the Ames impact occurred about 370 million years ago, meaning it was not part of the mysterious Ordovician bombardment once linked to a possible ring of debris around Earth. Instead, the impact coincided closely with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.

mix_items.title: Your gut bacteria may reveal how fast your brain is aging
mix_items.summary: A UCLA study links faster brain aging to specific gut bacteria and chemical byproducts, with older-looking brains also associated with poorer memory, focus, and mood. The findings suggest that biological signs of brain aging may appear decades before obvious symptoms and could eventually make the gut a target for prevention.

mix_items.title: Diet drinks work as well as water for weight loss, major trial finds
mix_items.summary: A two-year randomized clinical trial involving 493 adults with overweight or obesity found that diet soft drinks were essentially as effective as water for long-term weight loss and weight maintenance. Participants drinking beverages sweetened with aspartame, acesulfame-K, or sucralose lost a similar amount of weight to those drinking water, while both groups also saw improvements in waist size, body composition, and several metabolic measures.

mix_items.title: Hidden stem cells may be fueling spinal stenosis
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a stem cell that appears to serve as a master source for tendon and ligament cells throughout the body. In lumbar spinal stenosis, these cells become unusually active and may drive the ligament overgrowth that squeezes spinal nerves and causes pain, numbness, and difficulty walking. Researchers found that reducing calcium signaling stopped this abnormal growth in mice.

mix_items.title: Scientists find new virus behind mysterious tick illness
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new tick-borne virus in China that causes flu-like illness and may account for previously unexplained cases of fever, fatigue, digestive problems, and low platelet counts. Most patients with ALTNV alone recovered, but coinfections with another dangerous tick-borne virus were linked to more serious complications.

mix_items.title: Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
mix_items.summary: A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.
